items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for.  PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line.  The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation.  This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an…

items.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. items.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.content: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. In the second run of Stanford’s CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and explain the patch to the person who might merge it. We invited Mihail, who teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, to celebrate one million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. He opens up the course syllabus and shows us which lessons survived contact with his own engineering team. Monaco built its agent workspaces, bought its code review tools, and gave an on-call agent access to Datadog and GitHub. We ask how he decides which tools his team needs to own. items.title: Controlling Biology - Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
items.content: Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. It is not hyperbole at all to say that his lab has been pushing the frontier of algorithms to understand multi-scale, multi-modal (”multiomics”), time-varying biological data. Indeed, he has shaped the large scale vision and data collection through his leadership at Helmholtz, various startups and probably at Biohub itself. Watch the full episode on YouTube…   Much of the recent attention in AI x Bio has been on protein and molecular design. The discussion cites new imaging and measurement capabilities, generating large data sets and making the data available for training AI. items.title: Why the Cyberpocalypse Might Hit China Harder
items.content: Chang Che is a writer and contributor to the New Yorker . In August, researchers at a California security firm used an OpenAI model to find a software bug in PHP, a programming language that undergird some seventy per cent of the world’s websites, including Wikipedia and WordPress. They alerted PHP’s developers, who quietly began working on a fix. By late October, the fix was ready, but before they could alert the world, the break-in attempts had begun. Days earlier, Amazon detected someone trying to hack into its servers; attacks code began circulating online. Some governments and companies began pulling websites down, rather than risk a security breach. One security firm described the flaws as some of the worst ever found in PHP, “and arguably in software history.” Before AI, the internet might have looked, to a hacker, like a worn-out bug screen. You could discern some holes with a keen eye, and that knowledge was reliably asymmetric—others probably didn’t know about the holes you found. Moreover, tunneling through the holes undetected took months or years of human labor, talent, and money. Now, with AI, the internet looks more like a block of Swiss cheese: the holes are obvious, anyone can, or will, see them, and the time and cost it takes to exploit these software flaws have plunged alarmingly fast . According to Google’s incident response team , the average time it takes for cyber criminals to exploit a new vulnerability is -7 days, meaning hacking attempts are “routinely occurring before a patch is even released.” A China Central Television (CCTV) feature about the PHP vulnerability discovered by cybersecurity firm Calif, with the aid of OpenAI models. Source . Hackers refer to unbeknownst software bugs like PHP as “zero-days” because a defender has had zero days to protect themselves upon its discovery. items.title: WarTalk: Kofman on Why Russia's Doing Badly
items.content: The ChinaTalk team is going to CoRL (the Conference on Robot Learning) in Austin! Reply to this email if you’d like to hang out between November 9th and 12th. We’re also doing karaoke on the 11th — RSVP here if you’d like to join! Ukraine and Russia have rebuilt their armies around drones, deception, and long-range strike. What should the U.S. military take from it? Michael Kofman joins WarTalk regulars Jordan Schneider, Justin McIntosh, and Tony Stark. We discuss: How the Starshield throttle grounded Ukraine’s mid-strike drones and jet-powered interceptors, and why no one, Ukrainians included, knows what Washington wants in exchange. How much leverage the U.S. still has over the war, and why Europe can’t replace America’s role in NATO. Why buying drones means nothing without drone platoons and companies to fight with them. Why no one owns the night anymore, and why the U.S. military has no culture of decoys. The difference between a lesson and an observation, and why wet-gap crossings are harder than Twitter thinks. What Congress should push on: force design, airbase hardening, and hard questions about how the U.S. plans to fight. Plus: the perks of being a military analyst and Oregon Trail merch. Starshield Gets Throttled Jordan Schneider: Michael Kofman, the leading analyst of his generation, has taught me more about this war over the past four years than anyone else. Reading Mike’s tweets and articles , and listening to his podcast The Russia Contingency , honestly got me into this field. Today we’ll cover recent developments in Ukraine, starting with the Starlink–Starshield drama and Operation Vivaldi, then broaden out to lessons from the war — and some meta-discussion about the discussion of lessons.
